Feluda.description: A private detective renowned for his intelligence and deductive skills, also known as Feluda.

Topshe.description: Feluda's cousin and the narrator of the stories, often assisting Feluda in his investigations.

Lalmohan Ganguli.description: A popular crime thriller writer who uses the pen name Jatayu and is a close companion of Feluda.

Mahitosh Sinha-Roy.description: A well-known shikari, writer, and owner of the Sinha-Roy Palace whose family history is central to the mystery.

Torit Sengupta.description: The secretary to Mahitosh Sinha-Roy whose death triggers the investigation; his brother handles his funeral arrangements.

Devtosh Babu.description: Mahitosh Sinha-Roy's elder brother, known for his extensive knowledge of history but suffering from mental health issues.

Laxmanbari.description: A fictitious place near the border of Bhutan, where the main events of the story occur.

Bhutan.description: A country in the Eastern Himalayas, bordering India, referenced as the location near Laxmanbari.

Rajputana.description: A historical region in northwestern India, now largely in Rajasthan, from where the Sinha-Roy family is said to have originated.

Bengal.description: A region in eastern India, home to the story's main characters.

Todar Mal.description: A historical figure, a finance minister in the Mughal Empire, mentioned as having led armies in Bengal.

Pathans.description: An ethnic group from the north-western region of the Indian subcontinent, referenced as historical adversaries.

Calcutta.description: Now called Kolkata, it is the capital of West Bengal and the starting point of the story.

West Bengal.description: A state in eastern India, where much of the story takes place.

Sunderbans.description: A large mangrove forest area in southern West Bengal, famous for its tigers.

Terai.description: A region of marshy grasslands at the base of the Himalayas, known for its forests.

Orissa.description: Now called Odisha, a state in eastern India, mentioned as a possible residence of Mahitosh Sinha-Roy.

Assam.description: A state in northeastern India, also mentioned as a possible residence of Mahitosh Sinha-Roy.

Dooars Forest.description: A forested region in northern West Bengal, near Bhutan, where Mahitosh Sinha-Roy lives.

Robert Scott.description: A British explorer of the Antarctic, referenced in a book dedication.

David Livingstone.description: A British explorer and missionary in Africa, referenced in a book dedication.

Einstein.description: Albert Einstein, the famous physicist, referenced in a book dedication.

Sir Edmund Hillary.description: A famous New Zealand mountaineer, referenced in a book dedication.

The Tiger and the Gun.description: A book written by Mahitosh Sinha-Roy, consulted by Lalmohan Babu.

New Jalpaiguri.description: A major railway station in northern West Bengal, where the characters arrive before heading to Laxmanbari.

Shonadeeghi.description: A village near Dhaka, mentioned as the ancestral home of the narrator's family.

Dhaka.description: The capital of Bangladesh, referenced as the location near Shonadeeghi.

Mymansinh.description: A region in Bangladesh, where the narrator's uncle managed an estate.

Madhupur.description: A forested area north of Mymansinh, known for wildlife.

Corbett.description: Refers to Jim Corbett, a famous British-Indian hunter and writer.

Kenneth Anderson.description: A well-known hunter and writer of adventure stories set in Indian jungles.

Royal Bengal tiger.description: The Royal Bengal tiger is a subspecies of tiger native to the Indian subcontinent, featured in the story as a significant presence and symbol of the region's wildlife.

Indian government.description: The central government of India, referenced in relation to the ban on hunting.

New Farakka.description: A railway station in West Bengal, passed by the characters on their journey.

Himalayas.description: A major mountain range in Asia, visible from the north of Laxmanbari.

Darjeeling.description: A hill station in West Bengal, mentioned as being north of Laxmanbari.

Teesta.description: A river in the eastern Himalayas, crossed by the characters en route to Laxmanbari.

Hasimara.description: A town near the Bhutan border, where Mahitosh Sinha-Roy owns a tea estate.

Forest Department.description: A government body responsible for managing forests and wildlife in India.

Kalbuni.description: A forest near Laxmanbari, once known for its tigers.

Sinha-Roy Palace.description: The mansion owned by Mahitosh Sinha-Roy, where the main events unfold.

zamindar.description: A zamindar is a hereditary landowner, often with feudal privileges, in colonial and pre-colonial India; 'zamindars' refers to multiple such landowners.

shikari.description: A shikari is a hunter, especially one who hunts big game in India; the plural form 'shikaris' refers to multiple hunters, often featured in the context of tiger hunting.

Babu.description: A respectful term of address for men in Bengal, often used after a name.

adivasi.description: A term for the indigenous tribal peoples of India.

sheaf.description: A bundle of papers or documents, often manuscripts.

divan.description: A long, low sofa without a back or arms, commonly used in India.

Shashanka Sanyal.description: Mahitosh Babu's childhood friend and timber business manager who brings news of the death.

Bankim Chandra Chatterjee.description: A renowned Bengali novelist and poet, author of 'Devi Chowdhurani'.

Devi Chowdhurani.description: A famous Bengali novel by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, set in Bengal and featuring a female protagonist.

Trisrota.description: An ancient or alternative name for the Teesta river, referenced in Bengali literature.

Jalpeshwar.description: A Shiva temple near the story's setting, significant for local religious gatherings.

Shivaratri.description: A major Hindu festival dedicated to Lord Shiva, marked by night-long worship and fairs.

Gaur.description: An ancient city in Bengal, historically significant and once ruled by Sultan Hussain Khan.

Hussain Khan.description: A historical figure, former Sultan of Gaur, known for destroying Hindu temples in Bengal.

Kalapahar.description: A historical figure associated with the destruction of Hindu temples in Bengal.

mango sherbet.description: A sweet, chilled beverage made from mango pulp, sugar, and water, popular in India.

machaan.description: A raised platform or cot, often used in India for hunting or as a lookout in forests.

shikar.description: The act of hunting, especially big game, in the Indian subcontinent.

Madhavlal.description: A professional shikari (hunter) who acts as a guide for the group and is experienced in jungle expeditions.

Adityanarayan.description: Mahitosh Babu’s grandfather, who went mad in his old age and is associated with the hidden riddle and the sword.

Sher Shah.description: A historical figure, Sher Shah Suri, who allegedly earned his title by beheading a tiger with a sword.

Bikaner.description: A city in Rajasthan, India, known for its historic fort and Rajput heritage.

Rajput.description: A member of a prominent warrior class in India, associated here with impressive swords in Bikaner fort.

Mughal.description: Refers to the Mughal Empire, which ruled large parts of India; mentioned in relation to binoculars and hunting traditions.

Sinha-Roy.description: Sinha-Roy refers to the prominent family in the story, whose history and secrets are central to the plot. The Sinha-Roys are known for their heritage and the Sinha-Roy Palace.

badshahs.description: A Persian-derived term meaning 'kings' or 'emperors', used for Mughal rulers.

mrigaya.description: A Sanskrit word meaning 'hunting', used for royal or traditional hunting expeditions.

kukris.description: A type of curved knife traditionally used by the Gurkhas of Nepal and northern India.

Bhot Raja.description: Refers to the king of Bhutan; 'Bhot' is an old term for Bhutan or Tibet in Bengali.

Raja of Bhutan.description: The monarch of Bhutan, a Himalayan kingdom neighboring India.

Nawab.description: A historical title for Muslim rulers or noblemen in South Asia, particularly during the Mughal era.

Yudhisthir.description: A major character from the Indian epic Mahabharata, known for his righteousness; his chariot's wheels not touching the ground is a famous mythological motif.

Simla.description: A hill station in northern India, now known as Shimla, popular for its colonial architecture and cool climate.

Odomos.description: A popular Indian brand of mosquito repellent cream.

clogs.description: Wooden-soled footwear, sometimes worn indoors in India for comfort or to reduce noise.

mosquito nets.description: Fine mesh nets used in India to protect sleepers from mosquito bites, especially in rural or forested areas.

veranda.description: A roofed, open-air porch or gallery common in Indian homes, often used for sitting or socializing.

Kanai.description: One of the three bearers, responsible for bringing morning tea to the group.

Mr Datta.description: A man from the Forest Department who accompanies the investigation party.

yoga.description: A physical, mental, and spiritual practice originating in ancient India.

bearers.description: Servants or attendants, often responsible for carrying luggage or performing household tasks.

Inspector Biswas.description: Inspector Biswas is the police inspector leading the official investigation into Mr Sengupta's death, often in rivalry with Feluda. He is also referred to as Mr Biswas.

Chandan Mishir.description: The chowkidar (watchman) of Mahitosh Babu's estate, who provides local information about the forest and the tiger.

Charminar.description: A popular Indian brand of cigarettes smoked by Feluda.

chowkidar.description: A watchman or guard, typically employed to look after property.

huzoor.description: A term of respect meaning 'sir' or 'master', used in Hindi and Urdu.

Coochbehar.description: A town in West Bengal, India, mentioned in the context of a book on its history.

Chopped Goddess.description: A temple mentioned as a landmark near the significant peepul tree.

Raju.description: A person mentioned as being responsible for the temple of the Chopped Goddess.

fakir.description: A term for a holy man or ascetic, often associated with Sufi or Hindu traditions.

Sengupta.description: The surname of Torit Sengupta and Mr Sengupta, central figures in the mystery.

peepul tree.description: The peepul tree (Ficus religiosa) is a sacred fig tree commonly found in India, often associated with religious and cultural significance and serving as a landmark in the story.

khaki.description: A light brown fabric commonly used for trousers and uniforms, especially in India.

man-eater.description: A term used in India for a tiger or other animal that has developed a habit of attacking and eating humans.

Mr Sapru.description: A renowned shikari (hunter) expected to arrive to deal with the man-eater tiger.

Jim Corbett.description: A famous British-Indian hunter and author known for hunting man-eating tigers and leopards.

Durga.description: A major Hindu goddess, often depicted with ten arms, worshipped for her power and protection.

nullah.description: A small stream or watercourse, often dry except during the rainy season.

pug mark.description: A pug mark is the footprint or track of an animal, especially a tiger, with 'pug marks' being the plural form commonly used in Indian English.

banyan.description: A large, spreading tree (Ficus benghalensis) native to India, known for its aerial roots.

krait.description: A highly venomous snake found in South and Southeast Asia.

stinging nettle.description: A plant with hairs that cause a stinging sensation when touched.

Head of the Forest Department.description: The chief official in charge of the forest area, visited by Mahitosh Babu and Mr Sanyal.

Jalpaiguri.description: A town in West Bengal, India, referenced as a travel destination.

Kurukshetra.description: A historic battlefield from the Indian epic Mahabharata, referenced metaphorically.

Archimedes.description: An ancient Greek mathematician, referenced for his famous exclamation 'Eureka!'.

Parvat Singh.description: A bearer who accompanies Mahitosh Babu on hunting expeditions and is responsible for carrying the rifle.

Maharaja.description: A title for a Hindu prince or king in India, here referring to the ruler of Coochbehar.

bed-tea.description: Morning tea served in bed, a common custom in Indian households.

Sambalpur.description: A city in Odisha, India, mentioned as the location where the tiger was killed in 1957.

mynahs.description: A type of bird native to South Asia, often referenced in Indian contexts.

airgun.description: A gun that uses compressed air to fire pellets, commonly used for shooting small game or target practice in India.
